query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) treatment of non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloys accelerates the decomposition of metastable Mg-rich solid solutions into a more uniform dispersion of fine intermetallic compounds. This microstructural refinement creates a modified phase distribution that promotes the in situ formation of protective oxide scales during high-temperature oxidation, while also altering localized electrochemical sites to change corrosion pathways.
generation.material_initial_state: An induction‐melted, non-equilibrium, metastable Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with heterogeneous Mg-rich solid solution regions interspersed with coarse intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled rapid SPS treatment—with rapid heating and precise temperature control under an inert atmosphere—to the alloy to trigger accelerated phase transformation and grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Comparison against a similarly composed alloy processed with conventional sintering (or no SPS) under identical overall thermal exposure; performance evaluated in air at high temperatures for oxidation and in a standardized saline solution for corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure and a more uniform dispersion of fine intermetallic compounds, particularly from the decomposition of metastable Mg-rich phases.
generation.mechanism: The SPS treatment promotes rapid atomic diffusion and non-equilibrium phase transformation, reducing the size and heterogeneity of Mg-rich regions. This results in intermetallic phases that, upon exposure to high temperatures, preferentially nucleate and grow a coherent oxide layer, while also altering the electrochemical landscape to potentially homogenize or change corrosion attack paths.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline conventional processing, the SPS-treated alloy will exhibit a more uniform and protective high-temperature oxide scale and altered (potentially improved or more predictable) corrosion behavior, owing to the refined and redistributed intermetallic microstructure.
generation.baseline: The untreated or conventionally sintered alloy with a larger, heterogeneous mixture of metastable and intermetallic phases, leading to less uniform oxidation and variable corrosion performance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for alloys with density below 6 g/cm³ and under SPS conditions that do not lead to complete equilibrium; it may not hold if extended thermal exposures eventually override the microstructural stability conferred by SPS.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature and stability of the refined intermetallic phases under prolonged high-temperature exposure remain uncertain, as does the net electrochemical impact on long-term corrosion behavior, which may depend on small variations in alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed by SPS under controlled conditions and one set produced by conventional sintering. Perform microstructural analyses (XRD, SEM, TEM) to assess phase distribution and grain size, then subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests (in air) and corrosion tests (using a standardized saline solution).
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase fraction (XRD, TEM)
Morphology, thickness, and uniformity of the oxide scale (SEM, XPS)
Corrosion rates and attack uniformity (electrochemical measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-treated alloy does not display a statistically significant refinement in microstructure with a higher fraction of fine intermetallic phases and no corresponding (or opposite) change in the oxidation scale quality and corrosion behavior relative to the conventionally processed sample, the hypothesis is falsified.
